c1:
Eight months of savings isn't eight months of runway. The clock starts the day you quit, and a bakery earns nothing while you find a site, negotiate the lease, fit it out, and get through permits and a health inspection. That stretch is rarely shorter than a few months and often runs past six. The number that matters is how long you can last after the doors open, and every step on that list you get done before handing in your notice is time you're not paying for.

It also depends on what the eight months covers. If it's your living costs, the start-up money has to come from somewhere else, and bakeries are expensive to start: ovens, mixers, proofers, refrigeration, ventilation and the fit-out run to tens of thousands if you take over a space that was already a bakery, and well into six figures from a bare shell. The business needs its own cushion for the months it loses money, too. If one pot of savings is paying for all of that, eight months gets short fast. And your own costs rise once the job stops paying for things like health insurance or pension contributions.

The date the money has to reach isn't break-even. It's the first month the bakery can pay you. Those can be a long way apart: a bakery can cover its rent, flour and staff while the owner takes nothing home, and that's common for the first year or longer. A business can be on track and still run you out of money.

The downside isn't capped at your savings, either. Commercial leases run for years, and landlords usually want a personal guarantee from a first-time owner. Equipment finance often comes with one too. If the bakery closes in month ten, the lease doesn't. A stable job is usually easier to replace than a guaranteed lease is to get out of.

And running a bakery is mostly not baking. It's early mornings, food costs, staffing and unsold stock at closing time, with the baking fitted in around them. Most of what's uncertain here can be tested while you still have a salary: whether people pay your prices, how much you can turn out in a day, whether you like the work at that pace. Market stalls, supplying a café, a commercial kitchen rented by the hour, weekend shifts in someone else's bakery. If you've already been selling for a while, a lot of this is answered. If you haven't, the list of things you can only learn by quitting is short.
c2:
The mandates are evidence about executives, not about output. Companies want people back for plenty of reasons that aren't productivity: a ten-year lease on a half-empty tower, managers who like seeing their teams, and the fact that a mandate thins headcount without anyone paying severance. The closest thing to a direct test I know of is Ding and Ma's study of S&P 500 firms. Mandates tended to follow a slump in the share price, financial performance didn't improve afterwards, and employee satisfaction fell. If offices were coming back because they make teams more productive, the results should have shown it.

"Every" doesn't hold either. Amazon and JPMorgan went to five days, but last I knew most of big tech had settled on three. That's a vote for hybrid, and two days at home is still remote work. Hybrid is also where the best evidence runs the other way. Nick Bloom's randomised trial at Trip.com gave graduate staff two home days a week. Performance reviews and promotions came out the same over the next two years, and quit rates fell by a third.

Your claim is strongest for fully remote work, and there it has real support. Data-entry workers in India randomly assigned to work from home were 18% less productive. Teams spread across distance produce fewer breakthrough papers and patents. Junior engineers get noticeably less feedback when they don't sit near their team. So fully remote costs something, mostly for juniors and for hard collaborative work. The five-day mandates, though, are mostly replacing hybrid, which is the arrangement with the best evidence behind it.
c3:
Picture a square with side x, so its area is x². Make the side a little longer, by a small amount h. The new area is (x + h)², and the extra comes in three pieces: a strip down one side (x by h), a strip along the top (x by h), and a little square in the corner (h by h). So the area grows by 2xh + h².

The derivative is the area gained per unit of length added, as the added length shrinks to nothing. Divide by h and you get 2x + h. Let h go to zero and you're left with 2x. That's exactly the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h in your textbook; the square is just that formula drawn.

Everything rests on dropping the corner, and "because it's tiny" isn't the reason. The strips are tiny too. What matters is how fast each piece shrinks. Halve h and the strips halve, but the corner quarters. Per unit of h, the strips are worth 2x however small h gets, while the corner is worth h, which goes to zero. A limit keeps the part that's proportional to h and throws away whatever shrinks faster.

The 2 isn't arbitrary either. It's the two edges the square grows along. A cube grows on three faces, each of area x², and the edge and corner bits vanish for the same reason as before, which is why x³ gives 3x². That's the power rule for whole-number powers, and the n out front is counting the same thing: how many directions the shape grows in.
c4:
Liking it is the wrong test at this stage. You've read it so many times you're not reading it anymore — you're recognising it. You know every turn before it arrives and every joke is on its fortieth telling, so nothing in there can land on you. "I can't tell" is what that's like from the inside. It's a fact about how close you are to the book, not about the book.

There's one version of it that does mean something. If the whole thing's gone flat, that's familiarity. If you keep steering around one chapter, or a particular character makes you wince every time they open their mouth, that's a note, and a specific one.

What gets a reader's eyes back is time, not effort. A few weeks without opening it, then one quick read in a different format, printed or on an e-reader, without fixing anything as you go. And "anymore" means it worked on you once, before you knew it by heart.
c5:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at one place and time. Today's rain. This afternoon's wind. Next Tuesday's heat.

Climate is the statistics of weather over decades. The standard window is 30 years. People often call it average weather. That's incomplete. Climate is the whole spread, not just the middle. Typical highs and lows. The number of floods. The worst heatwaves. The extremes do most of the damage. A small shift in the average makes them far more common.

The sharpest difference is in prediction. Weather forecasts stop being reliable after about ten days. The cause is chaos: tiny errors in today's measurements grow fast and swamp the forecast. Climate can still be projected decades out. That isn't a contradiction. A climate projection makes no claim about any particular day. It describes the shape of the spread. A single dice roll is unpredictable. The average of ten thousand rolls isn't. Loaded dice move that average in a predictable direction. Greenhouse gases are the loading.
c6:
Twice is a lot.

That's a real question. Stopping is a real answer to it. So is going again. So is a break first. None of them has to be picked tonight. A result this fresh drowns out everything else.
